claims.text: Controlled oxygen incorporation enhances local chemical ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local chemical ordering produces nanoscale ordered clusters in HfNbTaTiZr.
The ordered clusters have lattice parameters distinct from those of the disordered matrix.
The ordered clusters have thermal-expansion coefficients distinct from those of the disordered matrix.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between clusters and matrix generates internal stresses during temperature changes.
The ordered clusters impede dislocation motion.
Ordered clusters reduce local lattice distortion by providing a more stable local structure.
Cluster-induced internal stresses influence the elastic modulus.
Cluster-induced internal stresses influence yield behavior.
The same ordering phenomenon explains creep, cold-work hardening, elastic-modulus variation, and aging-induced hardening.
The as-cast starting alloy is homogeneous and has a random solid-solution structure.
Aging at 600–800 °C promotes nanoscale chemical ordering.
Dislocation activity is minimal from 0 to 200 K, so thermoelastic properties dominate in that regime.
Creep, plasticity, and aging effects are prominent from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen-doped and aged specimens will have greater hardness than as-cast oxygen-lean specimens at lower temperatures.
Oxygen-doped and aged specimens will have a greater elastic modulus than as-cast oxygen-lean specimens at lower temperatures.
Oxygen-doped and aged specimens will have lower tensile-creep rates at 1250 °C because clusters obstruct dislocation motion.
Oxygen-doped and aged specimens will exhibit measurable internal thermal stresses during thermal cycling or simulated composite solidification.
The magnitudes of the mechanical and thermoelastic effects will correlate with the measured degree of ordering.

contradictions.description: The stated high-temperature validity range ends at 1200 K, but the central creep prediction and test are at 1250 °C, approximately 1523 K, outside that boundary.

A distinct 0–200 K regime is claimed as part of the hypothesis, but the proposed modulus and thermal-expansion measurements cover only 293–1100 K and therefore do not test that low-temperature regime.
